assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Avogadro constant (N_A)
items.clue: The number of particles per mole.

items.label: Pressure
items.clue: The perpendicular force on a surface per unit area.

items.label: Real gas
items.clue: Its molecules have non-zero volume and attract one another weakly.

items.label: Molar mass (M)
items.clue: Kilograms (or grams) of a substance per 6.02 × 10²³ of its particles.

questions.stem: A student pushes on a horizontal table top through a flat pad of area 8.0 cm². The force exerted by the pad on the table is 40 N, directed at 30° to the vertical. What pressure does the pad exert on the table?
questions.explanation: Only the component perpendicular to the table produces pressure. The vertical component is 40 cos 30° = 34.6 N, and A = 8.0 cm² = 8.0 × 10⁻⁴ m², so P = 34.6 ÷ 8.0 × 10⁻⁴ = 4.3 × 10⁴ Pa.

questions.stem: A cylinder contains 0.64 kg of oxygen gas, which consists of O₂ molecules. The molar mass of oxygen atoms is 16 g mol⁻¹, and N_A = 6.02 × 10²³ mol⁻¹. How many oxygen molecules are in the cylinder?
questions.explanation: The molar mass of O₂ is 2 × 16 = 32 g mol⁻¹ = 0.032 kg mol⁻¹, so n = 0.64 ÷ 0.032 = 20 mol. Then N = nN_A = 20 × 6.02 × 10²³ = 1.2 × 10²⁵ molecules.

questions.stem: Which of the following is an assumption of the kinetic model of an ideal gas?

options.text: All the molecules move with the same speed, which increases with temperature.
Molecules lose a small amount of kinetic energy in every collision with one another.
Molecules exert no forces on one another except during collisions.
The molecules are packed closely together and fill most of the container's volume.

questions.explanation: This is one of the model's assumptions. Together with point-particle molecules, elastic collisions of negligible duration and random motion, it defines the ideal gas; it also means an ideal gas has no intermolecular potential energy.

questions.stem: For a fixed mass of gas, the ideal gas law PV/T = constant can be derived from three empirical gas laws. Which statement of those three laws is correct?

options.text: PV is constant at constant θ; V/θ is constant at constant P; P/θ is constant at constant V (θ in °C)
PV, V/T and P/T each stay constant (T in K), whatever happens to the remaining variable
PV is constant at constant T; V/T is constant at constant P; P/T is constant at constant V (T in K)
PV is constant at constant T; VT is constant at constant P; PT is constant at constant V (T in K)

questions.stem: A rigid storage tank of internal volume 200 dm³ contains an ideal gas at a pressure of 3.00 × 10⁵ Pa and a temperature of 27 °C. R = 8.31 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹. What amount of gas is in the tank?

options.text: 2.7 × 10² mol
2.4 × 10⁴ mol
2.4 × 10¹ mol
2.4 × 10³ mol

questions.explanation: Convert to SI: V = 200 dm³ = 0.200 m³ and T = 300 K. Then n = PV/(RT) = (3.00 × 10⁵ × 0.200) ÷ (8.31 × 300) = 24 mol = 2.4 × 10¹ mol.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly explains how a gas exerts a pressure on the walls of its container?

options.text: The weight of the molecules presses down on the container, mostly on its base.
Each molecule's momentum changes as it rebounds from a wall, so it exerts a force on the wall.
The molecules repel one another, and this repulsion pushes outwards on the walls.
Molecules give their kinetic energy to the walls, and this energy is the pressure.

questions.explanation: The wall exerts a force on each molecule to reverse its perpendicular velocity (a momentum change of 2mv for an elastic rebound), and by Newton's third law the molecule exerts an equal and opposite force on the wall. The total force from all collisions per unit area is the pressure.

questions.stem: A container holds 8.0 g of helium, a monatomic gas of molar mass 4.0 g mol⁻¹, at 27 °C. Treat helium as an ideal gas. R = 8.31 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹. What is the internal energy of the helium?
Under which conditions does a real gas behave most nearly as an ideal gas?

options.text: High temperature, low pressure and low density
Low temperature, low pressure and low density
High temperature, high pressure and high density
Any temperature and pressure, provided the gas is helium

questions.explanation: At low pressure and density the molecules are far apart, so their own volume and their mutual attractions are negligible; at high temperature their kinetic energy is large compared with the intermolecular potential energy. These are the conditions assumed by the model.

questions.stem: A sealed container holds a gas at a pressure of 1.0 × 10⁵ Pa. Which statement about this pressure is correct?

options.text: The gas presses mainly on the base of the container, because gas pressure acts downwards.
Pressure is a vector, so the pressures acting on opposite walls of the container cancel out.
The gas exerts a force of 1.0 × 10⁵ N on each wall, whatever the area of that wall.
The gas pushes perpendicular to every wall, exerting 1.0 × 10⁵ N on each square metre of wall.

questions.explanation: Pressure is force per unit area, so F = PA: every 1 m² of wall receives a force of 1.0 × 10⁵ N, directed perpendicular to the wall. Because the molecules move randomly in all directions, this is true for the top, the sides and the base alike.

questions.stem: At room temperature and atmospheric pressure, measurements on helium agree closely with PV = nRT. A student concludes: 'Helium is an ideal gas.' Which evaluation of this conclusion is correct?

options.text: Justified: helium is monatomic and unreactive, and this makes it one of the ideal gases.
Not justified: helium atoms collide with one another, but ideal gas molecules do not collide.
Justified: agreement with PV = nRT shows that every assumption of the model is exactly true for helium.
Not justified: helium is a real gas that the model approximates closely under these conditions.

questions.stem: Air in a sealed syringe has a volume of 60 cm³ at a pressure of 1.00 × 10⁵ Pa and a temperature of 17 °C. The plunger is pushed in quickly until the volume is 20 cm³, and the air warms to 47 °C. Treat the air as an ideal gas. What is its new pressure?
questions.explanation: Using P₁V₁/T₁ = P₂V₂/T₂ with T in kelvin: P₂ = 1.00 × 10⁵ × (60/20) × (320/290) = 3.31 × 10⁵ Pa. Both the compression and the warming raise the pressure.

questions.stem: A flask of volume 250 cm³ contains an ideal gas at a pressure of 1.0 × 10⁵ Pa and a temperature of 300 K. k_B = 1.38 × 10⁻²³ J K⁻¹, R = 8.31 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹ and N_A = 6.02 × 10²³ mol⁻¹. How many molecules are in the flask?
